text: Thomas Callister Hales, born on June 4, 1958, is an American mathematician specializing in representation theory, discrete geometry, and formal verification. In representation theory, he is known for his work on the Langlands program and the proof of the fundamental lemma over the group Sp(4), with many of his ideas incorporated into Ngô Bảo Châu’s final proof of the fundamental lemma. In discrete geometry, he resolved the Kepler conjecture on sphere packing density, the honeycomb conjecture, and the dodecahedral conjecture. In 2014, he announced the completion of the Flyspeck Project, which formally verified the correctness of his proof of the Kepler conjecture. He earned his Ph.D. from Princeton University in 1986 with a dissertation titled The Subregular Germ of Orbital Integrals. Hales taught at Harvard University and the University of Chicago and worked at the University of Michigan from 1993 to 2002. In 1998, he submitted a paper on the computer-aided proof of the Kepler conjecture, a centuries-old problem stating that the most space-efficient way to pack spheres is in a tetrahedral arrangement, with graduate student Samuel Ferguson as his collaborator. In 1999, he proved the honeycomb conjecture and noted that it may have been considered by mathematicians before Marcus Terentius Varro, as referenced by Pappus of Alexandria in Book V. After 2002, Hales became the University of Pittsburgh's Mellon Professor of Mathematics. In 2003, he began work on the Flyspeck Project to formally verify his Kepler conjecture proof, which relied on computer calculations and used the proof assistants HOL Light and Isabelle. The Annals of Mathematics accepted the proof in 2005 but was only 99% confident in its correctness. In August 2014, the Flyspeck team’s software confirmed the proof as correct. In 2017, Hales initiated the Formal Abstracts project to provide formalized statements of key results from mathematical research papers in the language of interactive theorem provers, aiming to leverage increased precision and interoperability while avoiding full formalization of all proofs, with long-term goals of building a corpus of mathematical facts for machine learning applications in automated theorem proving. Hales collaborated with Koundinya Vajjha on a conjecture of Karl Reinhardt regarding the smoothed octagon having the lowest maximum packing density among centrally symmetric convex shapes in the plane; although they did not prove Reinhardt’s conjecture, in 2024 they claimed to have proven a related conjecture of Kurt Mahler: that the boundary of an extreme convex domain consists of line segments and arcs of hyperbolae. Hales was an invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians in 2002, won the Chauvenet Prize in 2003, the R. E. Moore Prize in 2004, a Lester R. Ford Award in 2008, and a Fulkerson Prize in 2009. He received the inaugural Robbins Prize from the American Mathematical Society in 2007 and became a fellow of the American Mathematical Society in 2012. He was invited to deliver the Tarski Lectures in 2019, with titles "A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture," "Formalizing mathematics," and "Integrating with Logic," and was awarded the Senior Berwick Prize of the London Mathematical Society in 2020.
